translation: At that time, in the age of Robinson and Rousseau, of English parks and pastoral poetry, one had seen in “original” man himself a kind of little lamb, peaceable and virtuous and only later corrupted by culture [Kultur]. Technical matters were overlooked entirely and in any case, compared with moral considerations, were not held worthy of attention. But the machine-technics [Maschinentechnik] of Western Europe, growing to gigantic proportions since Napoleon, with its factory towns, railways and steamships, finally compelled people to pose the problem seriously. [1] What does technics [Technik] mean? What meaning does it have within history, what value in the life of men, what moral or metaphysical rank? There were numerous answers to this, but at bottom they can be reduced to two. On the one side were the idealists and ideologues, the latecomers of the humanist classicism of Goethe’s time, who despised technical things and economic questions altogether as standing outside and beneath culture. Goethe, with his great sense for everything real, had tried in the second Faust to penetrate into the deepest depths of this new world of facts. But already with Wilhelm von Humboldt there begins the philological view of history, estranged from reality, according to which one in the end reckoned the rank of a historical epoch by the number of pictures and books produced in it. A ruler possessed significance only if he proved himself as a patron [Mäzen]. Whatever else he was did not come into consideration. The state was a constant disturbance of true culture, which went on in lecture halls, scholars’ studies and studios; war was an improbable [?: incredible] barbarism from past times; and the economy [Wirtschaft] [2] was something prosaic and stupid, which one looked past, although one made use of it daily. To name a great merchant or engineer alongside poets and thinkers was almost lèse-majesté against “true” culture. Let one look at Jacob Burckhardt’s “Reflections on World History” with this in mind. But that was the standpoint of most academic philosophers [Kathederphilosophen] and even of many historians, down to the literati and aesthetes of today’s great cities, who consider the making of a novel more important than the construction of an aircraft engine.
notes: Bracketed numerals [1], [2] are page markers in the source text, retained. Burckhardt's title is 'Weltgeschichtliche Betrachtungen'.

relevance.reason: The passage describes the idealist contempt for technics as the first of two nineteenth-century answers to what technics means; it says nothing about whether one society can adopt another's machinery without its ways of life (Q33).

Strasser, Vikings and Normans (1928). 12 For what migrated across from Spain, Portugal and France as well were certainly for the most part descendants of the conquerors of the Migration Period [Völkerwanderung]. What remained behind was the human stock that had already outlasted Celts, Romans and Saracens. 13 Compare the life of workers around 1700 and 1900, and the standard of living of urban workers in general with that of peasants. [74] In fact, however, neither the heads nor the hands can change anything in the destiny [Schicksal] of machine-technics [Maschinentechnik], which has developed out of an inner necessity of the soul [seelenhafter Notwendigkeit] and is now ripening towards its completion, its end. We stand today on the summit, at the point where the fifth act begins. The last decisions are being made. The tragedy is closing. [74] Every high culture is a tragedy; the history of man as a whole is tragic. But the sacrilege [Frevel] and fall of Faustian man is greater than anything Aeschylus and Shakespeare ever beheld. The creation rises up against the creator: as once the microcosm man rose against nature, so now the microcosm machine revolts against Nordic man. The lord of the world becomes the slave of the machine. It forces him, us, and indeed all without exception, whether we know and will it or not, in the direction of its course. The fallen victor is dragged to death by the careering team [Gespann].

translation: Everything organic succumbs to the spreading organization. An artificial world permeates [78] and poisons the natural one. Civilization [Zivilisation] has itself become a machine, which does or wants to do everything in the manner of a machine. People now think only in horsepower. They no longer see a waterfall without converting it in thought into electrical power. They see no land full of grazing herds without thinking of the exploitation of its stock of meat, no fine old handicraft of an indigenous [urwüchsigen] population without the wish to replace it by a modern technical process. Whether it has a meaning or not, technical thinking wants realization. The luxury of the machine is the consequence of a compulsion of thought [Denkzwang]. The machine is in the last resort a symbol, and, like its secret ideal, the perpetuum mobile, a necessity of soul and intellect [seelisch-geistige], but not a vital one. In many ways it is beginning to contradict economic practice. Disintegration is already announcing itself on every side. In the end the machine cancels its own purpose through its number and its refinement. In the great cities the automobile has, through its sheer numbers, robbed itself of its effect, and one gets on faster on foot. In Argentina, Java and elsewhere the simple horse-plough of the small holders proves economically superior to the great motors [79] and is displacing them again. Already in many tropical regions the coloured peasant with his primitive way of working has become a dangerous competitor of the modern technical plantation enterprise of the whites. And the white industrial worker in old Europe and North America is beginning, with his work, to become questionable.

translation: It is folly, as was the fashion in the 19th century, to talk of the threatening exhaustion of the coal deposits within a few centuries and of its consequences. That too was materialistic thinking. Apart from the fact that already today petroleum and water power have been drawn upon as inorganic reserves of energy of the greatest extent, technical thinking would very soon discover and open up quite other sources as well. But it is not at all a question of such spans of time. West European-American technics [Technik] will come to an end sooner. No trivial circumstance such as a shortage of materials would be able to halt this tremendous development. So long as the thought at work in it is at its height, it will always know how to create the means for its ends. But how long will it remain at its height? Merely to maintain the present stock of technical [80] processes and installations at the same level, there are needed, let us say, 100,000 outstanding heads [Köpfe]: organizers, inventors and engineers. They must be strong, even creative talents, enthusiastic for their cause and trained for it over years with iron diligence and at great cost. In fact, for 50 years most of the strong talents among the youth of the white peoples have felt a predominant inclination precisely for this profession. Even the boys played with technical things. In the urban strata and families whose sons chiefly come into consideration here, there were prosperity, a tradition of intellectual professions and refined culture, the normal preconditions for the formation of this ripe and late product, technical thinking.

relevance.reason: The passage argues that Western technics depends on a supply of trained talent formed in particular urban strata, but it does not address whether another society can adopt the machinery without its ways of life (Q33).

translation: This has been turning ever more clearly for decades, in all countries with large and old industry. Faustian thinking is beginning to grow tired [satt] of technics. A weariness is spreading, a kind of pacifism in the struggle against nature. People turn to simpler forms of life closer to nature; they go in for sport instead of technical experiments; they hate the great cities; they [81] want to get out of the compulsion of soulless activities, out of the slavery of the machine, out of the clear and cold atmosphere of technical organization. Precisely the strong and creative talents turn away from practical problems and sciences and towards pure speculation. Occultism and spiritualism, Indian philosophies, metaphysical broodings of Christian or pagan colouring, which were despised in the time of Darwinism, surface again. It is the mood of Rome in the time of Augustus. Out of weariness of life people flee from civilization into more primitive parts of the world, into vagabondage, into suicide. The flight of the born leaders from the machine is beginning. Soon only talents of the second rank, latecomers of a great age, will be available. Every great entrepreneur observes the decline in the intellectual qualities of the rising generation. But the magnificent technical development of the 19th century had been possible only on the basis of a constantly rising intellectual level. Not only decline, but even standstill is dangerous and points to an end, however many well-trained hands may be ready for work. But how do matters stand with these? The tension between [82] leaders’ work [Führerarbeit] and executing work [ausführende Arbeit] has reached the degree of a catastrophe. The importance of the former, and the economic value of every genuine personality within it, has become so great that for most people it is no longer visible and comprehensible from below. In the other, the work of the hands, the individual is now wholly without significance. Only number still has value. The knowledge of this unalterable situation, which is inflamed, poisoned and financially exploited by egoistic speakers and writers, is so desolate that a revolt against the role which the machine, not its owner, assigns to most people is human enough. There begins, in countless forms, from assassination through the strike to suicide, the mutiny of the hands against their destiny, against the machine, against organized life, finally against everyone and everything. The organization of work, as it has lain for millennia in the concept of acting together [Tun zu mehreren] 16, and which has as its basis the distinction between leaders and led, between heads and hands, is being dissolved from below. But “mass” is only a negation, namely of the concept of organization, nothing that would be viable on its own. [83] An army without officers is only a superfluous and lost heap of men. 17 A jumble of brick rubble and iron fragments is no longer a building. This mutiny all round the earth threatens to abolish the possibility of technical-economic work. The leaders can flee, but the led, who have become superfluous, are lost. Their number means their death.

translation: But the third and gravest symptom of the beginning collapse lies in what I should like to call the betrayal of technics [Verrat an der Technik]. It concerns things that everyone knows, but that are never seen in the context which first reveals their fateful meaning. The immense superiority of Western Europe and North America in the second half of the last century in power of every kind, economic, political, military and financial power, rests on an undisputed monopoly of industry. Great industries existed only in connection with coal deposits in these Nordic countries. The rest of the world was a market, and colonial policy always worked in the direction of opening up [84] new regions of sale and raw materials, not of production. There was coal elsewhere too, but only the “white” engineer could have opened it up. We were in sole possession not of the materials, but of the methods and of the brains trained to apply them. On this rests the luxurious standard of living of the white worker, who in comparison with the coloured 18 possesses princely earnings, a circumstance that Marxism suppressed, to its own ruin. This is taking its revenge today, when from this quarter the problem of unemployment is thrown into the course of development. The wage of the white worker, today a danger to his life, rests for its height exclusively on the monopoly that the leaders of industry had erected around him. 19 Then, at the end of the century, the blind will to power begins to commit decisive errors. Instead of keeping technical knowledge secret, the greatest treasure the “white” peoples possessed, it was boastfully offered to all the world in all the colleges, in speech and print, and people were [85] proud of the admiration of Indians and Japanese. The well-known “dispersal of industry” [Industriezerstreuung] sets in, partly also from the consideration that production had to be brought nearer to the buyer in order to obtain greater profits. Instead of the export exclusively of products there begins the export of secrets, of processes, methods, engineers and organizers. Even inventors emigrate. Socialism, which would like to harness them to its yoke, drives them away. All the “coloured” peoples looked into the secret of our strength, grasped it and exploited it. Within 30 years the Japanese became technical experts of the first rank and in the war against Russia demonstrated a superiority in military technics from which their teachers could learn. Today industrial regions have arisen or are forming everywhere, in East Asia, India, South America, South Africa, which on account of their low wages represent a deadly competition. The irreplaceable privileges of the white peoples have been squandered, thrown away, betrayed. The opponents have caught up with their models and perhaps, with the cunning of coloured races and the over-ripe intelligence of ancient civilizations, surpassed them. Wherever there is coal, petroleum and water power, a [86] new weapon can be forged against the heart of Faustian

translation: culture [Kultur]. Here begins the revenge of the exploited world against its masters. With the countless hands of the coloured peoples, who work just as skilfully and far less demandingly, the foundation of white economic organization is shaken. The accustomed luxury of the white worker compared with the coolie becomes his doom. White labour itself becomes superfluous. The huge masses on the Nordic coal, the industrial plants, the invested capital, whole cities and districts threaten to succumb to the competition. The centre of gravity of production is shifting irresistibly, now that the World War has also put an end to the respect of the coloured peoples for the white man. That is the ultimate reason for the unemployment in the white countries, which is not a crisis but the beginning of a catastrophe. For the coloured peoples, however (the Russians are always included here), Faustian technics is no inner need. Only Faustian man thinks, feels and lives in its form. It is necessary to his soul; not its economic consequences, but its victories: navigare necesse est, vivere non est necesse. For the “coloured” it is only a [87] weapon in the struggle against Faustian civilization [Zivilisation], a weapon like a tree branch in the forest, which one throws away when it has served its purpose. This machine-technics will end with Faustian man and will one day be shattered and forgotten: railways and steamships just as once the Roman roads and the Chinese Wall, our giant cities with their skyscrapers just as the palaces of ancient Memphis and Babylon. The history of this technics is rapidly approaching its inescapable end. It will be consumed from within, like all great forms of any culture. When and in what manner, we do not know.
